name: Certificate Chain
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Who Vouches for the Vouchers
lesson.summary: A certificate chain links an end-entity X.509 certificate through one or more issuing certificate authorities up to a trusted root, so trust in a single website borrows from trust in the authorities that signed for it.
lesson.body:
An X.509 certificate is a digitally signed document that binds an identity, such as a domain name, to a public key. It states, in effect, that whoever holds the matching private key controls that domain. It also carries other fields worth naming, such as the issuer, the validity period, and the algorithm used to create the signature, but the identity binding is the part that matters most here. A certificate is only useful if you can trust the signature on it, and that signature was created by a certificate authority, an organization whose job is to verify identities before issuing certificates. This raises an obvious question: what makes the certificate authority's own signature trustworthy? The answer is a certificate chain.

In practice, browsers and operating systems rarely trust a certificate authority directly for every certificate it issues. Instead, a small number of highly protected root certificate authorities sit at the top, and they issue certificates to intermediate certificate authorities, which in turn issue the end-entity certificates that websites actually present. When your browser connects to a website, the server sends not just its own certificate but the chain: its certificate, signed by an intermediate, whose certificate was signed by a root. The browser verifies each signature in sequence, checking that the intermediate's certificate was properly signed by the root it claims, and that the end-entity certificate was properly signed by that intermediate.

Walk through a concrete example. A browser visits a shopping site and receives a certificate for that site's domain, issued by, say, an intermediate certificate authority belonging to a large certificate issuer. The browser already has that issuer's root certificate stored in its trust store, but the presented chain shows an intermediate in between. The browser checks that the intermediate certificate carries a valid signature from the root, using the root's public key, and that the site's certificate carries a valid signature from the intermediate, using the intermediate's public key. If both signatures check out and neither certificate has expired or been revoked, the browser accepts the chain and displays the padlock.

This layered structure exists for practical reasons. Root certificate authorities keep their signing keys offline and heavily guarded, since compromising a root key would be catastrophic. Intermediates, which sign certificates far more frequently, absorb the operational risk, and if an intermediate is ever compromised it can be revoked and replaced without touching the root at all.

The certificate chain is, structurally, a short hash chain of signatures rather than hashes: each link's validity depends on the link above it, and breaking trust anywhere in the chain breaks everything below it. A missing intermediate, an expired link, or a broken signature at any point invalidates everything below it, no matter how correct the rest of the chain looks. Where the chain terminates, at a certificate nobody else signs, is the subject of the next chapter.
